title: How Epilepsy Works
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant (with guest producer Ramsey) explain epilepsy: its history of stigma from the Code of Hammurabi and witch-hunt handbooks through Hippocrates and 18th-century French neurologists, the brain's electrical "traffic jam" mechanism, focal vs. generalized seizures, auras, the three seizure phases (pre-ictal/aura, ictal, post-ictal), outdated terms petit mal and grand mal, first aid during a seizure and when to call 911 (status epilepticus), the six-plus epilepsy syndromes, triggers such as strobe lights and reflex epilepsy, diagnosis via EEG, CT and MRI, febrile and pseudoseizures, treatments including medication, the vagus nerve stimulator, surgery and the ketogenic diet, SUDEP, and living with epilepsy. The episode ends with listener mail about marathon running highs versus marijuana highs.

segments.title: Intro and history of epilepsy stigma
segments.summary: The hosts introduce epilepsy and how movies oversimplify seizures. They then cover ancient views, from Code of Hammurabi and demonic explanations to Hippocrates' brain-based view, medieval witch-hunting, laws barring people with epilepsy from marrying, and contagion beliefs until the 18th century.

segments.title: What happens in the brain and auras
segments.summary: The hosts describe a brain's electrical overload during seizures, with neurons firing in big peaks and valleys. They distinguish focal from generalized seizures, simple versus complex focal seizures, loss of consciousness, and auras, which can precede seizures by days.

segments.title: Three phases of a seizure
segments.summary: The hosts cover the three seizure phases: pre-ictal aura, ictal middle phase including drop attacks and injury risk, and the post-ictal recovery phase, which can include frustration, embarrassment, and shame.

segments.title: Types of generalized seizures
segments.summary: The hosts explain outdated terms petit mal and grand mal, now absence and tonic-clonic seizures, plus myoclonic, clonic, and tonic seizures. They note children and people over seventy-five are most likely to have epilepsy, and the French neurologists who began studying it.

segments.title: First aid during a seizure and status epilepticus
segments.summary: The hosts list what not to do, such as putting objects in the mouth, and what to do: protect from injury, clear the area, roll onto the side, loosen clothing, and stay nearby. Call 911 if a seizure lasts five minutes or more, if seizures repeat without regaining consciousness, or if the person is pregnant.

segments.title: Epilepsy syndromes and triggers
segments.summary: The hosts review several epilepsy syndromes: benign rolandic epilepsy, juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, reflex epilepsy triggered by flashing lights and touch, and temporal lobe epilepsy. They also discuss frontal lobe epilepsy.

segments.title: Causes, diagnosis, and seizure mimics
segments.summary: The hosts cover symptomatic, idiopathic, and cryptogenic causes. They discuss febrile seizures, pseudoseizures linked to psychological distress, and seizure mimics such as hypoglycemia. They then describe diagnosis with EEG, induced seizures, CT, and MRI.

segments.title: Treatment, surgery, and living with epilepsy
segments.summary: The hosts discuss anti-seizure medication and side effects, the vagus nerve stimulator, surgery to remove seizure-causing brain regions, corpus callosotomy and Julian Jaynes's bicameral mind idea, intractable epilepsy, SUDEP, the ketogenic diet, daily-life challenges, and famous people with epilepsy.

segments.title: Listener mail on marathon highs and sign-off
segments.summary: Listener mail discusses marathon runner's high versus marijuana highs, including a listener's ultramarathon hitting-the-wall story. The hosts close by inviting listeners to share their experiences with epilepsy.
